# Mahāsāropama Sutta (MN 29 (PTS MN i 192))

**ID:** MN 29 (PTS MN i 192)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Mahāsāropama Sutta
**PTS:** MN i 192
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0201m.mul2.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Mahāsāropama Sutta* ("The Longer Simile of the Heartwood") is the twenty-ninth discourse of the Majjhima Nikāya [Buswell & Lopez 2014]. The discourse was delivered by the Buddha at Mount Vulture Peak near Rājagaha shortly after Devadatta's departure and secession from the Sangha [Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli & Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Hazra 1994]. Prompted by Devadatta's pursuit of personal fame, gain, and honor through supernormal attainments, the Buddha warns the mendicants against becoming complacent or intoxicated with intermediate spiritual gains [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2005; Buswell & Lopez 2014; Schober 1997; Wijayaratna 1990].

Using the simile of a seeker gathering timber who mistakes twigs and leaves, outer bark, inner bark, or sapwood for core wood, the Buddha illustrates how practitioners may settle for worldly gain and honor, moral discipline, concentration, or knowledge and vision (*ñāṇa-dassana*), exalting themselves and disparaging others [Buswell & Lopez 2014; Narasabho 1971; Pye 1978; Webster 2005]. The sutta stresses that none of these intermediate achievements constitutes the final purpose of the holy life; rather, the ultimate goal and true heartwood is unshakeable deliverance of mind (*akuppā cetovimutti*) [Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli & Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- Full parallels: EA 43.4 提婆達
- Resembling parallels: MN 30 (PTS MN i 198) Cūḷasāropama Sutta

**Sources**

- [Bhikkhu Bodhi 2005] Bhikkhu Bodhi, ed., In the Buddha's Words: An Anthology of Discourses from the Pali Canon (2005) — Context on a clansman going forth and falling for intermediate gains.
- [Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli & Bhikkhu Bodhi 1995] Bhikkhu Ñāṇamoli and Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Middle Length Discourses of the Buddha (1995) — Setting at Vulture Peak after Devadatta's departure and emphasis on unshakeable deliverance.
- [Buswell & Lopez 2014] Robert E. Buswell Jr. and Donald S. Lopez Jr., The Princeton Dictionary of Buddhism (2014) — Setting, Devadatta context, Ekottarikāgama parallel, and heartwood simile outline.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Context regarding Devadatta's secession and monks tempted by gifts and fame.
- [Kingsbury 2002] Paul Kingsbury, Chronology of the Pali Canon: The case of the aorists (2002) — Discussion of the textual relationship with the Cūḷasāropama Sutta.
- [Narasabho 1971] Phra Maha Singhathon Narasabho, Buddhism: Guide to a Happy Life (1971) — Note on success in concentration, self-exaltation, and disparaging others.
- [Pye 1978] Michael Pye, Skillful Means: A Concept in Mahayana Buddhism (1978) — Alternative title and breakdown of progressive stages of spiritual practice.
- [Rogell 2003] Sharda Rogell, Pressing Out Pure Honey: A Practitioner’s Study Guide (2003) — Note on tree parts in the simile and the close match with MN 30.
- [Schober 1997] Juliane Schober, ed., Sacred Biography in the Buddhist Traditions of South and Southeast Asia (1997) — Context regarding Devadatta's desire for fame and honors.
- [Webster 2005] David Webster, The Philosophy of Desire in the Buddhist Pali Canon (2005) — Discussion of the compound ñāṇa-dassana in the sutta.
- [Wijayaratna 1990] Mohan Wijayaratna, Buddhist Monastic Life According to the Texts of the Theravāda Tradition (1990) — Observation that the holy life does not aim at profit, honor, or fame.
